column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 13: Love for your brother what you love for yourself

column2: Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: “None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim reported it.
This hadith is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Qatādah, from Anas. Muslim's wording is “until he loves for his neighbour — or for his brother —”, with the narrator unsure which he said.
Imam Aḥmad recorded it with the wording: “A servant does not attain the reality of faith until he loves for people the good that he loves for himself.”

This narration explains the meaning of the one recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: what is denied is that he has reached the reality and the full extent of faith. Faith is often denied of someone when some of its pillars and obligations are missing, as in his words ﷺ:

“The fornicator is not a believer at the moment he fornicates, the thief is not a believer at the moment he steals, and the drinker is not a believer at the moment he drinks wine,” and his words: “He does not believe whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.”
Scholars have differed over whoever commits major sins: is he to be called a believer whose faith is deficient, or is he not to be called a believer at all,
so that one says only, “He is a Muslim, not a believer”? There are two views on this, and they are two reported positions of Imam Aḥmad.
As for whoever commits minor sins, the name of faith does not leave him altogether. He is a believer whose faith is deficient, and his faith decreases in proportion to what he has committed.
The view that one who commits major sins is called a believer whose faith is deficient is narrated from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, and it is the view of Ibn al-Mubārak, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and others.
The view that he is a Muslim and not a believer is narrated from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, and some have stated that it is the preferred view among Ahl al-Sunnah.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: The light of faith is stripped from the fornicator.
Abū Hurayrah said: Faith is stripped from him and stays above him like a canopy; when he repents, it returns to him.

ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah and Abū al-Dardāʾ said: Faith is like a shirt, which a person puts on at one time and takes off at another. Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) and others said the same. The meaning is

that when he completes the traits of faith he puts it on, and when he falls short in any of them he takes it off. All of this refers to complete and perfect faith, from whose obligations nothing is missing.

The point is that among the obligatory traits of faith is that a person love for his believing brother what he loves for himself, and dislike for him what he dislikes for himself. If that leaves him, his faith is diminished by it.
It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to Abū Hurayrah: “Love for people what you love for yourself, and you will be a Muslim.” Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded it.

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Muʿādh, that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about the best of faith, and he said: “The best of faith is that you love for Allah's sake and hate for Allah's sake, and keep your tongue busy with the remembrance of Allah.” He asked: And what else, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “That you love for people what you love for yourself, dislike for them what you dislike for yourself, and say what is good or keep silent.”
The Prophet ﷺ made entry into Paradise depend on this trait.

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him), Yazīd ibn Asad al-Qasrī said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: “Do you love Paradise?” I said: Yes. He said: “Then love for your brother what you love for yourself.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever would love to be kept away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise, let his death come to him while he believes in Allah and the Last Day, and let him treat people as he would love to be treated.”

Also in it, Abū Dharr said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: “Abū Dharr, I see that you are weak, and I love for you what I love for myself. Do not take command over even two people, and do not take charge of an orphan's property.”
He forbade him this only because of the weakness he saw in him, and he ﷺ would want the same for every weak person. He himself took charge of people's affairs only
because Allah had given him the strength for it and commanded him to call all creation to His obedience and to take charge of governing their religion and their worldly affairs.

It has been narrated that ʿAlī said: The Prophet ﷺ said to me: “I am pleased for you with what I am pleased with for myself, and I dislike for you what I dislike for myself. Do not recite the Qurʾān while you are in a state of major ritual impurity (janābah), nor while bowing, nor while prostrating.”
Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ was once selling a donkey of his, and a man asked him: Would you be happy with it for me?

He said: If I were happy with it, I would not be selling it. By this he indicated that he would be happy for his brother only with what he would be happy with for himself. All of this is part of the sincere counsel (naṣīḥah) owed to the generality of Muslims, which is itself part of the religion, as was explained in its place.

We have already cited the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The likeness of the believers in their mutual love, affection and mercy is that of a single body: when one part of it is in pain,

the rest of the body shares its fever and sleeplessness.” It is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. This shows that the believer is troubled by what troubles his believing brother and grieved by what grieves him.
The hadith of Anas that we are now discussing shows that the believer is gladdened by what gladdens his believing brother, and wants for his believing brother the good that he wants for himself.
All of this comes only from a heart that is wholly free of rancour, deceit and envy. Envy makes the envier hate that anyone should surpass him in some good, or even equal him in it,

because he loves to stand out from people by his merits and to keep them to himself. Faith requires the opposite: that all the believers should share with him in the good Allah has given him, without any of it being lessened for him.
Allah the Exalted has praised in His Book those who desire neither exaltation in the land nor corruption. He said:
“That is the Home of the Hereafter: We grant it to those who desire neither exaltation in the land nor corruption” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:83].
Ibn Jarīr narrated, with a chain that is open to question, that ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

A man may be delighted that the strap of his sandal is finer than his companion's, and so he comes under His words: “That is the Home of the Hereafter: We grant it to those who desire neither exaltation in the land nor corruption, and the [good] outcome belongs to the God-fearing” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:83].

Something similar is narrated from al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ on this verse. He said: [Such a person] does not love for his sandals to be finer than anyone else's, nor his sandal straps finer than anyone else's.

It has been said that this applies when he wants to boast over others, not when he merely wishes to look well. ʿIkrimah and other exegetes said about this verse: Exaltation in the land is arrogance and seeking honour and standing with whoever holds power in it; corruption is acting in disobedience.

There are reports indicating that one who dislikes being surpassed by anyone in good looks is not sinning. Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) and al-Ḥākim in his Ṣaḥīḥ recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said:

I came to the Prophet ﷺ while Mālik ibn Murārah al-Rahāwī was with him, and I arrived as he was saying: O Messenger of Allah, I have been given the share of good looks that you see, and I would not like anyone at all to outdo me by so much as a pair of sandal straps or more. Is that not wrongful pride (baghy)?
He said: “No, that is not wrongful pride. Wrongful pride is to spurn — or he said: to scorn — the truth and to look down on people.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ; in his hadith it has “arrogance” in place of “wrongful pride”.
So the Prophet ﷺ denied that the man's dislike

of being surpassed by anyone in good looks was wrongful pride or arrogance, and he explained arrogance and wrongful pride as spurning the truth and looking down on people. Spurning the truth means holding oneself above it and refusing, out of arrogance, to accept it when it goes against one's desires.
That is why one of the Salaf said: Humility is to accept the truth from whoever brings it, even someone young. Whoever accepts the truth from the one who brings it,
whether young or old, and whether he likes him or not, is humble; and whoever refuses to accept the truth because he holds himself above it is arrogant.
Looking down on people means despising and belittling them, and it comes from looking at oneself with the eye of perfection and at others with the eye of deficiency.

In short, the believer ought to love for the believers what he loves for himself and dislike for them what he dislikes for himself. If he sees some deficiency in his Muslim brother's religion, he strives to set it right.

One of the righteous among the Salaf said: Those who love Allah looked by the light of Allah and were tender towards those who disobey Allah. They hated their deeds yet were tender towards them, so as to draw them away from what they did by admonishing them, and they feared for their bodies from the Fire.

The believer is not truly a believer until he is pleased for people with what he is pleased with for himself. If he sees in someone else a merit by which that person surpasses him, he wishes for the like of it himself;
and if that merit belongs to the religion, this is good. The Prophet ﷺ wished for himself the rank of martyrdom.

He ﷺ also said: “There is no envy except in two cases: a man to whom Allah has given wealth and who spends it through the hours of the night and the day, and a man to whom Allah has given the Qurʾān and who recites it through the hours of the night and the day.”

Of the man who saw someone spending his wealth in obedience to Allah and said, “If I had wealth, I would do with it as he has done,” he said: “The two of them are equal in reward.” If, however, the merit is a worldly one, there is no good in wishing for it, as the Exalted said:

“So he went out before his people in his finery. Those who desired the life of this world said, ‘If only we had the like of what Qārūn has been given! He is indeed the owner of a great fortune.’ But those who had been given knowledge said, ‘Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for whoever believes and does righteous deeds’” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:79–80].

As for the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, “Do not covet that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others” [al-Nisāʾ 4:32], this has been explained as envy: a man's wishing for the very family and wealth his brother has been given, and that they should pass to him.

It has also been explained as wishing for what is ruled out by the Sharīʿah or by divine decree, such as women wishing to be men, or to have the merits men have, whether religious, such as jihād, or worldly, such as inheritance, blood money (ʿaql), testimony and the like. It has also been said that the verse covers all of this.

For all that, the believer ought to grieve over religious merits he has missed. That is why he has been commanded to look, in matters of religion, to those above him, and to compete for that with all his effort and ability, as the Exalted said:

“For that let the competitors compete” [al-Muṭaffifīn 83:26]. He does not dislike that anyone should share in it with him; rather, he loves for all people to compete in it and urges them to do so, and this belongs to the complete fulfilment of sincere counsel towards one's brothers.
Al-Fuḍayl said: If you love for people to be like you, you have not fulfilled sincere counsel towards your brother — so how is it when you love for them to be beneath you?!

He means that fulfilling sincere counsel towards them is to love for them to be above oneself. This is a lofty station and a high degree of sincere counsel, but it is not obligatory; what the Sharīʿah commands is only that he love for them to be like him.
Even so, when someone surpasses him in a religious merit, he strives to catch up with him and grieves over his own shortcoming and his failure to keep pace with those who have gone ahead —

not out of envy of them for the bounty Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has given them, but out of competing with them, with emulation (ghibṭah), and with grief at his own soul for falling short and lagging behind the ranks of those who went ahead.

The believer ought always to see himself as falling short of the high ranks. He gains two precious things from this: he strives to seek merits and to increase in them, and he looks at himself with the eye of deficiency. From this it follows that he loves for the believers to be better than him,

because he is not content for them to be in a state like his, just as he is not content with his own soul as it is, but strives to set it right. Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ said to his son: As for your father, may Allah not multiply his like among the Muslims.
How could someone who is not pleased with himself love for the Muslims to be like him, when he wishes them well?
Rather, he loves for the Muslims to be better than him, and he loves for himself to be better than he is.

If a person knows that Allah has favoured him over others with some merit, and he tells of it for a religious benefit, as a way of speaking of Allah's blessings and while seeing himself as falling short in gratitude,

that is permissible. Ibn Masʿūd said: I know of no one more knowledgeable of the Book of Allah than I am. Nor does this prevent him from loving for people to share with him in what Allah has singled him out with.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: I pass by a verse of the Book of Allah and wish that all people knew of it what I know. Al-Shāfiʿī said: I wish that people would learn this knowledge

without any of it being attributed to me. And ʿUtbah al-Ghulām, when he wanted to break his fast, would say to one of his brothers who knew of his devotions: Bring me out some water or a few dates to break my fast with,
so that you may have a reward like mine.
